study.title: Joshua 13 The land still to be shared and the inheritance that comes from the Lord
study.overview: The chapter shows the transition from conquest to the distribution of the earth. Joshua is old, and the Lord reminds him that there was still much land to be taken; yet he commands the territory already conquered to be divided among the tribes. The text also resumes, in detail, the lands given earlier by Moses to Reuben, Gad and half Manasseh, and concludes with the repeated statement that Levi did not receive territorial portions, because the Lord himself would be his inheritance. Thus, the chapter emphasizes that the possession of the land is not an autonomous right of Israel, but a gift of God, administered according to his promise and order.

outline.title: Joshua aged and the land still remaining
outline.explanation: God reminds Joshua of his advanced age and the fact that there were still unachieved regions, especially areas linked to the Philistines, Canaanites, Sidonians and Amorites. The text does not deny divine fidelity; it shows that the promise has already begun to be fulfilled, but there were still stages to be lived in the history of Israel.

outline.title: Order to share and Levi's inheritance
outline.explanation: Even with land still to be subdued, the Lord sends to share what has already been granted between nine and a half tribes. The chapter also highlights the inheritance already received on the other bank of the Jordan and pauses: Levi will not receive territory, for his inheritance is the sacrifices of the Lord.

outline.title: The inheritance of Reuben
outline.explanation: The text describes the limits and cities of the portion of Reuben, linked to the region delivered by Moses after the defeat of Seom and his allies. He also recalls the death of Balaam, showing that the conquest involved judgment on Israel's specific enemies.

outline.title: The inheritance of Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh
outline.explanation: The following are listed the territories of Gad and half of Manasseh, including towns, peasants and regions of Bashan and Gilead. The chapter ends as it began: Levi had no territorial inheritance, because the Lord himself was his portion.

study.context: This chapter belongs to the phase in which Israel, already established on earth, moves from war to the organization of tribal inheritance. The text itself explains that part of the territory to the east of the Jordan had already been given by Moses before his death, and that the distribution between the tribes would be made by divine order. The lists of borders serve to record concretely the fulfillment of the promise made to the patriarchs and to preserve the tribal organization of Israel.
study.theology: Joshua 13 teaches that God's faithfulness precedes and sustains the inheritance of his people. The earth is presented as a gift, not as a human autonomous conquest: God orders, grants and distributes. At the same time, the chapter shows the tension between promise and process: there is still land for possessing, but this does not invalidate what has already been given. Theologically, the text also highlights the distinction between territorial inheritance and priestly inheritance. Levi does not receive a lot of land because his portion is the Lord himself, which points to a spiritual priority above material possession. Moreover, the chapter suggests community responsibility: the inheritance must be distributed in an ordained manner, according to the divine word, and not according to mere human convenience.

scholarViews.insight: Tribal portions give geographical reality to God's covenant with Israel and express the fulfillment of the promise made to the patriarchs; the land is a gift because it belongs to the Lord.

God commands Joshua to divide what has already been conquered, even before the whole land is subdued; the people must receive what they have with obedient confidence, without expecting to possess all at once.
The repeated claim that Levi received no territorial inheritance points out that his portion was the Lord, and not a distribution of land like that of the other tribes.

questions: How does the order to divide the earth, even with regions not yet conquered, challenges my tendency to expect perfect conditions before obeying God?
What does it mean, in practice, to say that the Lord is the inheritance of someone, above goods, position or material security?
How can God's faithfulness in the past give me confidence to deal with promises still in the process of fulfillment?
study.practice: This week, identify an area of your life in which God has given you something enough to obey, even if it is not yet all you want. Instead of focusing only on what is missing, take a concrete step of gratitude and fidelity: organize, share, serve or manage what you have received. Also take aside time to pray with the psalm of Levi's heart: recognize the Lord as his greatest inheritance, above any earthly gain.
study.uncertainty: The chapter provides extensive lists of borders and cities, but not all of them can be safely identified only from the text and the notes given. The exact historical references of some geographical names remain uncertain, and therefore were treated descriptively, without reconstructions beyond what the notes support. It is also not possible to affirm with absolute precision the extent of some areas only with this material.
